questions.explanation: A jump from 4.4 to 5.9 in a single year that lands exactly on the day the probe was replaced is the classic signature of a method artefact, because a stream's nitrate does not step-change on a rebuild day, and the only thing that changed on that date was the measurement. Running the old and new probes side by side for a period of overlap gives the offset directly, and once it is known the whole series can be placed on one scale and the long-term trend read properly. Option B is the belief that a sharp change is evidence of a real event, which is true often enough to be seductive and is precisely why the coincidence with a rebuild has to be checked before it is believed. Option C throws away the years that carry the trend, and the offset they contain is exactly what is needed to interpret the years that follow. Option D is the reasonable-sounding defence of the rebuild, and it fails because two instruments built to the same specification still need not agree, which is what calibration is for.
questions.hint: Ask what changed on the day of the jump, apart from the stream.

answer.exemplar: Replication reduces the random part of uncertainty, because averaging n independent readings shrinks the standard error as one over the square root of n, so going from four to sixteen replicates halves it from 0.4 times the single-reading spread to 0.2 times it. It leaves a systematic offset exactly where it was, since every replicate of an instrument that reads 60 percent carries the same 40 percent shortfall and averaging biased numbers leaves their bias intact. A good answer therefore separates the two error sources by name, computes the standard error term for both sample sizes, shows that the sixteen-replicate figure is the tighter estimate, and then says the point plainly: it is a more precise estimate of a value that is still wrong by the same 40 percent. It should add that the remedy is calibration or standardisation against a reference of known value, which attacks the bias directly and is not a substitute for replication, and that neither remedy substitutes for the other.

questions.explanation: A strong answer names the two error sources and treats them separately, then shows the arithmetic: the standard error term falls from 0.8 to 0.4 as n rises from 4 to 16, so the 16-replicate mean is the tighter estimate, while the 40 percent offset is present in every replicate and is untouched by averaging. It should state the conclusion without hedging, that the improvement is real but applies to precision only, and that the measured value remains 40 percent wrong in both cases. It should then name the correct remedy for the bias, calibration against a reference, and note that replication and calibration attack different errors and neither replaces the other. An answer that says only that more replicates give a better estimate, or only that bias cannot be fixed, misses the whole point, which is that one of the two got better and the other did not move.
questions.hint: Split the reported result into the true value, a bias term and a scatter term.
questions.learningObjective: explain why replication reduces random error but not systematic bias

questions.explanation: An intercalibration needs a common material to anchor the comparison and the laboratories' own materials to test whether they agree on real differences, and a certified reference sediment analysed by everyone does the first job while each laboratory's own sediments do the second. If the reference results cluster, method bias is bounded and the spread in the real samples is genuine sample variability, whereas if the reference results scatter, no comparison of the real samples means anything because the measuring sticks are of unknown length. Option B compares six different materials with six different methods and attributes every difference to the material, which is the fundamental error this exercise is built to prevent. Option C replaces the comparison with a decree, which removes the only evidence that could have found a bias. Option D measures repeatability within each laboratory, which is a different question and one each laboratory can answer alone.
questions.hint: You need one thing every laboratory measures in common, and one thing that stays local.

questions.explanation: Well depth is continuous, so a survey in which all four hundred values sit exactly on a half-metre lattice has been rounded rather than measured at that resolution, and the gap in the record between 3.0 and 3.5 is the signature. Rounding is not a harmless clerical convenience, because every statistic computed on a snapped variable inherits the snapping, so a test for wells shallower than 3.2 metres and a mean depth are both distorted by values the instrument never reported. The tempting belief is that neat values must be true, and the second temptation is that a neat instrument produces neat readings, when a tape measure or a sounder reads continuously and the discreteness entered in the notebook. Option D's remedy is the worst of the four, since it converts a rounding artifact into a systematic doubling of every value, which is a real bias rather than a recorded uncertainty.
questions.hint: Ask whether the quantity being recorded can physically take only these values.

questions.explanation: Ten sediments recovering between 55 and 64 percent of a known spike, all sitting near 60, is a tight cluster around one wrong level, and a tight cluster around a wrong level is a bias, not scatter. Bias is systematic: it has a sign, a cause, usually a matrix effect or a preparation loss, and it survives any number of additional spikes. Scatter has no centre to cluster around and does average down. Option B treats a nine-point range as if it were a random spread, and the diagnosis here is that the spread is far too small and too one-sided to be random. Option C is the general belief that any shortfall is by definition random, which would leave systematic loss permanently undiagnosed. Option D is the most dangerous of the four, because a method that consistently finds 60 percent still ranks samples correctly and is therefore easy to live with right up until someone needs the absolute number.
questions.hint: Ask whether the recoveries scatter around a level, or cluster tightly around a wrong level.

questions.explanation: On day 1 the reading matches the standard, and on day 400 it still matches it, so the interval estimate around that mean is vanishingly narrow and the value itself is unambiguously correct. Repeating a measurement narrows the confidence interval around the number the method produces and does nothing whatsoever to the difference between that number and the truth, because the same offset is in every replicate. This is why an internal quality control that only repeats samples can look perfect for a method that is wrong every time, and it is the reason a reference of known value has to be measured alongside the unknowns. Option B asserts that replication removes a fixed offset, which is the most consequential misconception in the whole area, because it is what licenses a laboratory to keep running an uncalibrated method. Option C confuses a narrow interval with a zero error bar, and option D draws a conclusion about future standards that says nothing about the present standard.
questions.hint: Ask what the 400 repeats actually re-measured, and what they could not re-measure.

questions.explanation: A range is the least informative summary a time series can have, because it discards the pairing of value to date that a trend is made of, so a threefold spread over twelve years is equally consistent with a steady decline, a single high outlier in the first year, or no change at all. Nothing in the abstract says whether the same sites were sampled each year, and a monitoring programme that migrates upstream as sites are rebuilt can manufacture a decline without anything in the environment changing. Option B is the belief that a large spread of numbers is itself a direction, which is the same confusion that makes a histogram look like a trend when the bars are sorted. Option C claims that attaching years to the values is sufficient, which holds only if the years came with a design that held sampling comparable, and that is exactly what the abstract has not told us. Option D is not a finding at all: a source's format says nothing about the strength of its evidence, and abstracts often carry the sharpest data in a report.
questions.hint: Ask what a range contains, and what a claim about direction needs that a range cannot supply.
